extracted.intended_audience: physicians/AMA members, health policy advocates, state medical societies, clinician stakeholders in federal health policy
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and summarizing the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) provisions that affect Medicaid, the ACA marketplaces, Medicare physician payment, and federal student loans, with emphasis on implementation requirements and policy changes that impact patient access and provider finance. Intended as a concise catalog of statutory changes and their practical implications for health care stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicaid: new administrative requirements and eligibility conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: "OBBBA creates new administrative requirements and conditions on eligibility (including work requirements) for patients seeking to enroll in or maintain Medicaid coverage."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMA notes these changes will affect enrollment and maintenance of coverage and may worsen patient access to care. See linked AMA summaries for details (e.g., Summary: Changes to Medicaid and CHIP enrollment, eligibility and cost-sharing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on states' use of provider taxes to finance Medicaid
rubrics_metrics.description: "[OBBBA] restricts states’ ability to use provider taxes to finance their Medicaid programs."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision limits a state's financing options for Medicaid, with likely fiscal and access consequences. AMA has published a specific summary: "Summary: Changes to Medicaid financing (PDF)".

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicaid redetermination frequency change
rubrics_metrics.description: OBBBA establishes a new requirement for states to redetermine the eligibility of certain Medicaid beneficiaries more frequently—on a six-month basis as opposed to annually.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMA submitted recommendations to CMS regarding forthcoming guidance on this change (letter, Dec. 1, 2025). AMA materials include a "Summary of select provisions and implementation dates" and a timeline for implementation across programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicaid community engagement (work) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: OBBBA requires states to condition Medicaid eligibility for certain beneficiaries on the satisfaction of community engagement requirements (also known as work requirements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMA engaged with CMS on this requirement (letter, March 9, 2026) and produced issue briefs addressing exemptions and hardship policies (e.g., "Issue brief: Medicaid work requirements' medical frailty exemption" and "Issue brief: Short-term hardship exemptions from Medicaid work requirements").

rubrics_metrics.name: ACA marketplaces: verification requirements for premium tax credits
rubrics_metrics.description: "OBBBA imposes verification requirements for patients receiving premium tax credits, including pre-enrollment verification requirements that will effectively end automatic re-enrollment for these patients."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMA emphasizes this will affect continuity of coverage for marketplace enrollees. The bill also interfaces with administrative rules (Marketplace Integrity and Affordability Final Rule); AMA published a timeline and a specific summary: "Summary: Changes to ACA marketplace eligibility, enrollment and affordability (PDF)".

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduled expiration of enhanced premium tax credits left unaddressed
rubrics_metrics.description: "OBBBA does not address the scheduled expiration of enhanced tax credits at the end of 2025."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMA and coalitions have urged congressional extension of enhanced advanced premium tax credits (letter Sept. 15, 2025). AMA also published an issue brief: "Extension of enhanced premium tax credits key to ACA marketplace affordability."

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal support for medical student loans: elimination and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: "OBBBA, in part, removes the ability for medical students to receive Federal Direct Stafford loans and Federal Direct PLUS Loans (medical students will still be able to access Federal Direct Unsubsidized Stafford loans), caps the amount that can be borrowed for school, and limits new federal student loan borrowers to only two repayment options."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AMA produced an analysis: "Federal student loans and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (PDF)" describing how these changes alter medical student financing and the practical effects on trainees and institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cap on medical student borrowing and restriction to two repayment options
rubrics_metrics.description: OBBBA places a cap on the amount that can be borrowed for school and limits new federal student loan borrowers to only two repayment options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constraints reduce borrowing flexibility for new medical students; AMA provides briefing materials and advocacy letters addressing consequences for the physician workforce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicare physician payment reform: temporary 2026 conversion factor update
rubrics_metrics.description: "OBBBA includes a temporary one-year 2.5% conversion factor update for 2026, replacing the original House bill that called for a 75% MEI inflation update in 2026 followed by an annual 10% MEI increase, leaving no permanent, inflation-adjusted payment fix."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute provides only a short-term payment increase and no permanent, inflation-indexed payment solution; AMA commentary and letters (e.g., May 20, 2025; June 20, 2025) document concerns about long-term physician payment stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elimination of pass-through entity tax (PTET) deduction in House bill (policy note)
rubrics_metrics.description: The House-passed version of the reconciliation bill eliminated the pass-through entity taxes (PTET) deduction; AMA signed on to a letter urging restoration of the PTET deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This item was part of earlier legislative versions and advocacy activity; AMA engaged with congressional leadership (letter, June 9, 2025) to restore the deduction. Included here as a notable tax/finance change tied to the reconciliation process.
